fields.claim_quote: If $f(1)=3$, then $P(1)$ gives $f(3)=1$.  Then, $P(3)$, $P(4)$, and $P(5)$ yield $f(4)=5$, $f(5)=4$, and $f(6)=5$, respectively.
fields.explanation: Proves every function with those three values violates the equation atn3; P3 instead forces f4=3.

fields.problem:
Title: Sequence : $f(f(n))+f(n+1)=2n$

Does there exist a function $f : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$  such that $f(f(n))+f(n+1)=2n$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ ?

My attempt :

Substitute $n=1$, $f(f(1))+f(2)=2$ so $f(f(1))=f(2)=1$ 

Substitute $n=2$, $f(f(2))+f(3)=4$ so $f(1)+f(3)=4$ 

Substitute $n=3$, $f(f(3))+f(4)=6$ 

Assume that there exists $k >1$ such that $f(k) \geq k$,

then $f(f(k-1))+f(k)=2k$, we have $f(f(k-1))<k$

0003 | If $f(1)=1$, then $P(2)$ gives $f(3)=3$.  Then, $P(3)$ gives $f(4)=3$.  By induction on the positive integer $k$, we can easily see that
0004 | $$f(2k-1)=2k-1\text{ and }f(2k)=2k-1$$
0005 | for every $k=1,2,3,\ldots$.  In other words,
0006 | $$f(n)=2\,\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1$$
0007 | for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$.
0008 | 
0009 | If $f(1)=2$, then $P(2)$ implies $f(3)=2$.  Then, $P(3)$, $P(4)$, and $P(5)$ lead to $f(4)=5$, $f(5)=4$, and $f(6)=5$.  It can be proven again by induction that 
0010 | $$f(3k-2)=3k-1\,,\,\,f(3k-1)=3k-2\,,\text{ and }f(3k)=3k-1$$
0011 | for all $k=1,2,3,\ldots$.  In other words,
0012 | $$f(n)=3\,\left\lceil\frac{n}{3}\right\rceil-1-\left\lfloor\frac{n\mod 3}{2}\right\rfloor$$
0013 | for $n=1,2,3,\ldots$.
0014 | 
0015 | If $f(1)=3$, then $P(1)$ gives $f(3)=1$.  Then, $P(3)$, $P(4)$, and $P(5)$ yield $f(4)=5$, $f(5)=4$, and $f(6)=5$, respectively.  We claim that, for all positive integers $k$,
0016 | $$f(3k+1)=3k+2\,,\,\,f(3k+2)=3k+1\,,\text{ and }f(3k+3)=3k+2\,.$$
0017 | However, this claim can be easily verified by induction on $k$.  Thus,
0018 | $$f(n)=3\,\left\lceil\frac{n}{3}\right\rceil-1-\left\lfloor\frac{n\mod 3}{2}\right\rfloor$$
0019 | for $n=4,5,6,\ldots$, with $f(1)=3$, $f(2)=1$, and $f(3)=1$.
